topStories.headline: Stay Back From the Water: Coastal Flood Advisory and Beach Hazards Statement in Effect at Ocean Beach Through Tuesday
topStories.dek: The National Weather Service has issued stacked warnings for the Sunset's coastline — tidal flooding through Tuesday and dangerous surf this weekend.
topStories.body:
The National Weather Service issued a Coastal Flood Advisory for San Francisco beginning Friday, October 9, running through 3 p.m. Tuesday, October 13. The agency warns that up to 1.2 feet of inundation above ground level is possible in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways, with high tides pushing water and waves farther up the beach than normal and potentially cutting off access to some low-lying coastal areas.

Layered on top of the flood advisory, NWS added a Beach Hazards Statement running from Saturday morning through Monday afternoon. The hazards statement warns of breaking waves up to 16 feet along the San Francisco coast, with increased risk of rip currents and sneaker waves. The agency says dangerous conditions are forecast along the shoreline and urges beachgoers to stay well back from the surf.

At the San Francisco tidal gauge, high tide on Saturday, October 10 is expected to reach 1.2 feet above normal — roughly 7.06 feet MLLW — at around 11:50 a.m. Similar readings are forecast for Sunday and Monday. The NWS notes that surge of up to 1.0 foot will enhance the astronomical tide during this period.

The warnings directly affect Ocean Beach and the Sunset Dunes Park promenade along the Great Highway. Residents and visitors are advised not to drive around barricades or through water of unknown depth. Park programming at Sunset Dunes scheduled for the weekend — including the Zumba session Saturday morning and the 2nd Sunday Serenades on Sunday — may see altered shoreline conditions; check organizer channels before heading out.

topStories.headline: Prop G Asks Voters to Reopen Great Highway to Cars on Weekdays — Opponents Say It Would Cost $14 Million and Gut the Park
topStories.dek: With mail ballots now going out, San Francisco voters face a November 3 decision on whether to restore weekday vehicle access to the Upper Great Highway.
topStories.body:
On November 3, San Francisco voters will decide on Proposition G, a citizen initiative that would reopen the Upper Great Highway to private vehicles from 4 a.m. Monday through 6 p.m. Friday, while keeping the road closed to cars on weekends and holidays. The measure would unwind Proposition K, the 2024 ballot measure that permanently closed the oceanside road and created Sunset Dunes Park.

Supporters submitted 15,924 signatures, and on July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified that the petition had more than the 10,615 valid signatures required. The proponent listed in filings with the Department of Elections is Richard Corriea, a retired SFPD commander, and the campaign is led by Great Highway for Everyone. Supporters argue that traffic injuries in the Sunset neighborhoods have risen since the closure, as commuters are diverted onto other nearby streets.

Opponents say the plan would require the city to remove park features including picnic areas, seating, and the skate park. A city analysis from the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency and the Recreation and Parks Department estimated the removal of those features would cost $14 million. Friends of Sunset Dunes notes that 60 percent of park visits happen on weekdays and that a majority of the Board of Supervisors oppose Proposition G, including Board President Rafael Mandelman, Matt Dorsey, Bilal Mahmood, Myrna Melgar, Danny Sauter, and Stephen Sherrill.

District 4 Supervisor Alan Wong has voiced support for the weekday-compromise approach. Mail-in ballots are being sent to registered voters in early October. Prop G needs a simple majority — 50 percent plus one vote — to pass.

topStories.headline: 562-Unit Safeway Redevelopment Near Ocean Beach Moves Forward Under State Streamlining, Sidelining Public Hearings
topStories.dek: State law has removed the project at 850 La Playa Street from the usual Planning Commission process, frustrating neighbors who gathered at a late-September community meeting.
topStories.body:
A plan to replace the Safeway at 850 La Playa Street — a 3.3-acre site at the far western edge of the city, one block from Ocean Beach — is proceeding under a state-streamlined approval process that bypasses the standard San Francisco Planning Commission hearing. The Richmond Review/Sunset Beacon reported on October 5 that the Planning Association for the Richmond hosted a community meeting at the end of September at St. John's Presbyterian Church on Lake Street, giving area residents a rare informal forum to weigh in.

According to Planning Association presenter Zachary Nathan, the two proposed buildings would stand about 85 feet tall at 721,000 square feet, containing 562 dwelling units and 280 residential parking spaces, with a unit mix of 124 studios, 188 one-bedroom apartments, 192 two-bedroom apartments, and 58 units with three or more bedrooms. All of the units would be rental housing. About 20 percent — 113 units — would be offered at below-market rate; of those, 30 would be priced at 50 percent of the Area Median Income and the remainder at 80 percent.

Because the project is being streamlined for approval under state density bonus law SB330, there is no requirement for a Planning Commission hearing where the public can give formal input, and it is also exempt from California Environmental Quality Act review. Developer Align Real Estate is working on behalf of Albertsons Companies, Safeway's parent, which owns the site. The retail space would grow from the current 37,340 to 63,000 square feet, preserving a Safeway on site. No construction timeline or store closure date has been announced.

moreNews.headline: Sunset's First 100% Affordable Family Housing Building Reached Full Occupancy in July
moreNews.body: The 90-unit building at 2550 Irving Street — the Sunset District's first 100-percent affordable family housing project — reached full occupancy in July 2026, SF YIMBY reported on July 24. Developed by the Tenderloin Neighborhood Development Corporation with the Mayor's Office of Housing and Community Development, the seven-story all-electric building serves households earning between 30 and 80 percent of the Area Median Income. Of the 90 homes, 22 are reserved for families exiting homelessness and 15 for formerly homeless veterans. The $63.4 million project includes a rooftop deck overlooking Golden Gate Park and the Marin Headlands, and ground-floor community space dedicated in part to the Sunset Chinese Cultural District.

moreNews.headline: All SF Libraries Closed Monday, October 12 for Indigenous Peoples' Day
moreNews.body: All San Francisco Public Library branches — including the Sunset Branch at 1305 18th Avenue and the Parkside Branch at 1200 Taraval Street — will be closed Monday, October 12 in observance of Indigenous Peoples' Day. Regular hours resume Tuesday, October 13.
